description: Planned IT-STE rule concepts produced by reviewed adaptation decisions. These entries are not normative rules.

targets.working_title: Admit general vocabulary and domain terms
targets.design_intent: Define how general words and IT-specific nouns and verbs enter the controlled vocabulary through documented meanings, contexts, and terminology authority.

targets.working_title: Use terms only as approved
targets.design_intent: Make approval specific to meaning, part of speech, form, and applicable context, including independent approval when one spelling functions as both an IT noun and verb. Check the definition and usage restrictions of the applicable IT lexical entry before use; approval in one sense or context does not approve other senses or contexts. Do not import ASD-specific dictionary restrictions as IT-STE vocabulary decisions.

targets.working_title: Use authoritative terms consistently
targets.design_intent: Require one authoritative name for each concept within its context while preserving exact external names and documented mappings between interface layers.

targets.working_title: Select clear international terms
targets.design_intent: Select the shortest unambiguous internationally understood term when no authority controls it, without prohibiting established or clearly defined IT terminology.

targets.working_title: Use American English spelling
targets.design_intent: Use American English as the canonical prose baseline unless a governing contract, specification, style guide, or other mandatory external directive requires another variety; always preserve quotations, proper names, localized examples, and externally controlled or machine-significant literals.

targets.working_title: Clarify multi-word technical terms
targets.design_intent: Make an already selected multi-word term clear in prose without changing authoritative or machine-significant names. Show modifier relationships with grammatical phrasing, write a long term in full at first use in each independently consumable unit, and introduce an unambiguous contextual alias or abbreviation only when it improves readability. Preserve established hyphenation, add hyphens only when standard spelling or grammar requires them, distinguish hyphens from dashes, and never substitute typographic dashes for syntax-controlled characters. Do not impose an absolute three-word limit or add hyphens to evade a length limit.

targets.working_title: Use simple and unambiguous verb constructions
targets.design_intent: Use the simplest verb construction that preserves the technical meaning. Prefer simple tenses and explicit clauses, but permit perfect or progressive aspect when sequence, duration, current activity, or present result matters. Distinguish states from passive actions, permit established IT nouns and clear modifiers that end in ing, and rewrite dense auxiliary or modifier chains. Preserve externally controlled and machine-significant text exactly.

targets.working_title: Prefer active voice and name the actor
targets.design_intent: Use active voice when the actor or responsible component matters. Permit passive voice when the actor is unknown, irrelevant, intentionally omitted for security, or less important than the affected object or state. In instructions, name the responsible actor or use a direct imperative. Never invent or misidentify an actor only to force active voice.

targets.working_title: Use direct verbs for actions
targets.design_intent: Use a direct approved verb for an action when it is clearer than a nominalization or a support-verb phrase. Keep nouns when they name concepts, states, interface labels, commands, fields, or other machine-significant elements, and preserve externally controlled text exactly.

targets.working_title: Write concise and concrete sentences
targets.design_intent: Write sentences that communicate one principal topic or action with enough concrete information to be accurate. Split a sentence when independent ideas or actions make it difficult to understand, but do not remove necessary conditions, constraints, identifiers, or relationships only to reduce length. Do not impose one universal word limit across procedural or descriptive IT content; a content profile can define and validate a local limit for a specific format or audience.

targets.working_title: Include words needed for clarity
targets.design_intent: In controlled prose, include all grammatically and semantically necessary words so that actors, actions, objects, conditions, and referents are unambiguous. An imperative can keep its understood reader subject, and a sentence does not need an object when its verb or meaning does not require one. Use articles and demonstratives where standard English and the intended specificity require them. Spell out contractions. Permit conventional fragments in headings, labels, tables, diagrams, CLI syntax, logs, source code, and other constrained content when context supplies the omitted grammar. Preserve quotations, externally controlled strings, and machine-significant text exactly.

targets.working_title: Use parallel lists for complex content
targets.design_intent: Use a list when it makes multiple items, alternatives, prerequisites, or actions easier to scan. Introduce the list clearly, make every item connect grammatically to its lead-in, keep items parallel, use an ordered list only when sequence or priority matters, and keep punctuation and item style consistent. Separate unlike content when one list would mix descriptions, commands, or logical levels. Follow the governing output format or style guide for presentation details.

targets.working_title: Connect related ideas explicitly
targets.design_intent: Use a clear transition when readers must understand sequence, contrast, cause, result, or another relationship between sentences. Reuse the same canonical key terms as anchors when they help readers connect related information across sentences or independently retrieved chunks. Do not replace a term with a synonym merely for variety, but do not add a connector or mechanical repetition when order and context already make the relationship clear. Prefer an explicit noun phrase to this, these, or another demonstrative when more than one antecedent is possible.

targets.working_title: Put one executable action in each step
targets.design_intent: Put each independently executable action in a separate procedural step so that readers and automation can follow, verify, resume, and report it independently. Keep multiple actions in one step only when they are simultaneous, atomic, conventionally inseparable, or immediately coupled to a required result or verification. Preserve an intentional transaction boundary and do not split a command, expression, or code example into artificial actions.

targets.working_title: Use the imperative for reader actions
targets.design_intent: Start an instruction to the reader with a direct imperative verb and keep the reader as the understood subject. Name the actor explicitly when a system, service, role, team, or automated agent performs the action. Do not add must to an imperative only for emphasis; express obligations, policy requirements, and safety or security constraints with the semantic form and severity required by the governing content type. Preserve literal commands and interface text exactly.

targets.working_title: State conditions before dependent actions
targets.design_intent: State a prerequisite or condition before the action that depends on it, and make the condition's scope unambiguous. For a short clause, use punctuation that clearly separates the condition from the command. For multiple or complex conditions, use separate sentences, a list, or an explicit control-flow structure. Do not hide a prerequisite after the action or make the reader undo work that should not have started.

targets.working_title: Keep required actions out of notes
targets.design_intent: Use a note only for supplemental information that helps the reader but is not necessary to complete the procedure correctly. Keep required actions, prerequisites, limits, acceptance criteria, expected results, and safety- or security-critical information in the main flow. Give warnings, cautions, requirements, and other semantic blocks their correct labels. A procedure must remain complete and executable when its notes are hidden or skipped.

targets.working_title: Present information in a reader-first sequence
targets.design_intent: Present purpose, scope, prerequisites, and core concepts before details that depend on them. Move from familiar or high-level information to new or specialized information, and expose optional detail progressively. Give each independently retrievable section, help topic, or LLM chunk enough local context to identify its subject and interpret its references without copying unrelated background into every unit. Keep one principal subject in each sentence when possible; when multiple subjects are necessary, state their relationship explicitly. Apply this sentence-level control consistently with ITSTE-R-0010.

targets.working_title: Keep each content block focused on one topic
targets.design_intent: Group related information in a paragraph or the equivalent structural block for the content type, and keep one primary topic in that block. Identify the topic early unless a heading, label, schema position, or container already makes it clear. Start a new block when the topic, reader task, retrieval boundary, or level of detail changes, or when length impairs scanning. Do not impose a universal six-sentence maximum; headings, reference entries, tables, cards, messages, and other constrained formats can provide equivalent topic boundaries without conventional paragraphs.

targets.working_title: Label risks using the governing classification
targets.design_intent: Select a risk label from an actual risk assessment and the governing classification policy. Consider physical harm, data loss, security compromise, and service disruption, including combined risks; do not downgrade a more serious risk because another consequence seems minor. Do not impose the aviation warning/caution distinction as a universal IT scale or equate risk labels with log levels or incident priorities without a documented mapping. Make the classification understandable in text rather than relying only on color or a symbol. Follow applicable publication and accessibility requirements instead of mandating uppercase formatting.

targets.working_title: Lead protective instructions with an action or condition
targets.design_intent: After the risk label, start a protective instruction with a clear preventive action or prohibition, or with a condition that the reader must evaluate first. State the required action explicitly rather than only saying be careful. Place the instruction before the hazardous operation, identify its scope and responsible actor when necessary, and keep it available with independently retrieved procedural content. Apply the condition-first principle consistently with ITSTE-R-0016 and do not hide required precautions in notes.

targets.working_title: Explain credible consequences of a risk
targets.design_intent: When a credible consequence is known and can be disclosed, explain the risk or possible result after the protective action or condition. Identify the affected people, data, system, or service and explain the consequence specifically enough to support the decision. Distinguish possible consequences from certain outcomes; do not invent causes, probabilities, or guarantees. If details are unknown or security-sensitive, state the actionable risk at an appropriate level without exposing secrets or unnecessary exploit details. An explanation does not replace the protective action.

targets.working_title: Use punctuation to clarify structure
targets.design_intent: Use standard English punctuation to make relationships and sentence boundaries clear. Prefer separate sentences or steps to complex semicolon constructions in prose, but do not impose a universal ban on semicolons. Follow the governing content profile where it restricts prose punctuation. Preserve punctuation in quotations, commands, source code, configuration, URLs, paths, and other syntax-controlled or externally controlled text exactly; prose guidance must not change executable meaning.

targets.working_title: Keep parenthetical information unambiguous
targets.design_intent: Use parentheses for clear references, identifiers, introduced abbreviations, step markers, or short explanations when they improve comprehension. Avoid dense or nested parenthetical prose. State required conditions, limits, and branch-selection criteria explicitly in the main instruction rather than hiding them in parentheses. Prefer an explicit singular or plural form or an applicable quantifier to compact forms such as item(s), and expand ambiguous parenthetical alternatives into explicit choices. Preserve parentheses and other delimiters in literal commands, code, schemas, and externally controlled text exactly.

targets.working_title: Define reproducible length metrics in content profiles
targets.design_intent: If a content profile applies length limits, define a reproducible measurement method, its version, and its scope. Specify boundaries for list lead-ins and items from document structure; a colon in IT syntax is not automatically a sentence boundary. Specify treatment of parenthetical text, numbers and units, abbreviations, identifiers, quotations, titles, headings, labels, proper names, hyphenated compounds, code, URLs, paths, and structural numbering. Do not automatically count arbitrary parenthetical or quoted passages as one word or conceal their complexity through exclusions. Distinguish words, characters, and LLM tokens; token budgets must identify the tokenizer and its version. Preserve exact literals and do not alter spelling, hyphenation, or document structure merely to game the metric. No universal ASD counting convention or 20/25-word limit is imposed on IT-STE.

targets.working_title: Rewrite sentences without changing technical meaning
targets.design_intent: Use a different sentence construction when a word-for-word replacement is ungrammatical, unclear, or changes the intended meaning. Preserve actors, actions, objects, negation, modality, conditions, sequence, quantities, limits, and technical relationships. Preserve quotations and machine-significant literals exactly. Split or reorganize prose, lists, and tables only when the same information and dependencies remain clear; check related text and references for unintended effects. If the source meaning is unclear, obtain clarification from an authoritative source or subject-matter expert rather than inventing missing facts.

targets.working_title: Approve multi-word verb meanings explicitly
targets.design_intent: Do not infer approval of a phrasal or other multi-word verb meaning from approval of its individual words. Admit an established IT expression only with a documented meaning, grammatical pattern, and applicable context, using the vocabulary controls in ITSTE-R-0001 and ITSTE-R-0002. Prefer a clearer direct verb when it preserves the same meaning, but do not impose a blanket ban on phrasal verbs or force an inaccurate one-word replacement for an established expression such as sign in. Preserve authoritative interface wording, literal commands, and identifiers exactly, and distinguish them from explanatory prose.

targets.working_title: Reuse wording when meaning and context match
targets.design_intent: Use the same authoritative terms and consistent sentence patterns for equivalent instructions or descriptions when meaning and context match. Apply terminology consistency through ITSTE-R-0003 and reuse reviewed wording or templates instead of introducing stylistic synonyms. Do not erase differences in actors, conditions, quantities, scope, timing, or effects merely to make sentences look alike. Preserve externally controlled interface text and machine-significant literals exactly. Keep descriptive text coherent as a whole rather than repeating a procedural template mechanically.
